title: Biggest Drinking Days of the Year (and How to Get Through Them)
excerpt: The biggest drinking days of the year, from New Year's Eve and Blackout Wednesday to St. Patrick's Day and the Super Bowl, with the risk each brings and one plan that works for all of them.
metaDescription: The biggest drinking days of the year, from New Years Eve to Blackout Wednesday, why each is risky, and a simple plan to stay safe and skip the hangover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no official, measured "biggest drinking day of the year." Nobody counts every drink Americans pour on a given date. The lists you see online come from beer and liquor sales data, bar and restaurant trade reports, and surveys, and they rank days differently depending on what they measure. Even so, the same handful of days shows up on almost every list: **New Year's Eve, the night before Thanksgiving (often called Blackout Wednesday), St. Patrick's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, and the Fourth of July**, followed closely by Mardi Gras, Cinco de Mayo, the Memorial Day and Labor Day weekends, Halloween, and the December holiday party season. This guide walks through each one, explains why drinking spikes on that day and what the specific risk is, and gives you one plan that works for all of them.

**The quick rules for any big drinking day:** decide how you're getting home before you take your first drink, eat a real meal beforehand, alternate every alcoholic drink with water, set a rough drink limit while you're still sober, and know the signs of alcohol poisoning so you can act fast if a friend is in trouble. Most of the harm on these days comes from the same few things: long sessions that start early, drinking on an empty stomach, losing count, and driving.

> **When to get help right away.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while passed out or barely conscious, has a seizure, has pale, bluish, or cold clammy skin, or is too confused to answer simple questions. Turn them on their side so they can't choke, stay with them, and don't let them "sleep it off" alone. Don't drive after drinking, and don't ride with a driver who has been drinking. If you're worried about your own drinking, a doctor is a good, private place to start.

## Why There's No Single "Biggest Drinking Day"

If you search "what day do people drink the most," you'll find confident answers that disagree with each other. That's not because someone is wrong. It's because they're measuring different things:

- **Retail sales.** Beer, wine, and spirits sales from stores spike in the days before big at-home events. By this measure, the run-up to the Fourth of July, Super Bowl Sunday, and the end-of-year holidays tend to stand out, because people are stocking coolers and party tables.
- **Bar and restaurant sales.** Bar trade groups and point-of-sale companies look at what's poured in bars. Here, nights like New Year's Eve, St. Patrick's Day, and Thanksgiving Eve rise to the top, because those are nights people go *out*.
- **Surveys.** Polls ask people which holidays they drink most on. These reflect habits and memory, not measured volume, and results vary with who's asked.
- **Harm data.** Emergency rooms, police, and traffic safety agencies look at the consequences: crashes, arrests, and alcohol-related emergencies. Holiday periods, especially around the Fourth of July and the end of December, are consistently flagged by US traffic safety officials as high-risk times for drunk driving.

So "biggest drinking day" can mean the biggest sales day, the busiest bar night, or the most dangerous day on the roads. They overlap, but they're not the same list. What matters for you is simpler: on any of these days, more people around you are drinking, sessions run longer, and the roads are riskier. That's worth planning for.

## The Biggest Drinking Days of the Year, One by One

Here are the days that appear most often, in calendar order, with what makes each one different.

### New Year's Eve (December 31)

New Year's Eve is the day most people name first, and it's the classic "biggest bar night of the year." It combines almost every risk factor at once: a late night that often starts with dinner and drinks and runs past midnight, champagne toasts on top of whatever you were already drinking, crowded venues, and a huge number of people trying to get home at the same time. Rideshare prices surge and taxis are scarce right after midnight, which is exactly when some people talk themselves into driving.

**The specific risk:** losing track. A glass of bubbly here, a shot at midnight, a cocktail at the next party, and you've had far more than you'd guess. Sparkling drinks may also be absorbed a little faster than still ones, which can make the effects sneak up on you.

**One tip:** book your ride home, or arrange to stay where the party is, before you go out. Plan to leave either well before midnight or well after, when demand eases. For the morning after, see our [New Year's hangover guide](/never-hungover/new-years-hangover).

### Super Bowl Sunday (early February)

Super Bowl Sunday is often cited as one of the biggest beer days of the year, and it's mostly an at-home event: watch parties with a cooler, snacks, and four-plus hours of game, pregame, and halftime. It's also a work-night drinking day for many people, since Monday morning comes right after.

**The specific risk:** steady, uncounted drinking over a long stretch, then driving home from a friend's house. US traffic safety campaigns run specific "don't drive drunk" messaging around the game for this reason.

**One tip:** decide your drink number before kickoff, count your cans (keep the empties in a pile instead of tossing them), and switch to water or soda by the fourth quarter if you're driving later. If you're hosting, set out food that actually fills people up, not just chips.

### Mardi Gras (Fat Tuesday, February or March)

Mardi Gras falls the day before Ash Wednesday, so the date moves each year. In New Orleans and a few other cities it's a weeks-long season of parades and street parties, with the biggest crowds on the final days. Elsewhere it's usually a themed bar night.

**The specific risk:** all-day outdoor drinking in crowds, often with "go cups" and no clear end point, plus walking long distances. Dehydration, getting separated from your group, and falls are common problems.

**One tip:** set a meeting point with your group and keep your phone charged. Eat a proper meal before the parades, not just street snacks, and drink water between every drink.

### St. Patrick's Day (March 17)

St. Patrick's Day is one of the busiest bar days of the year in the US and in many other countries. Because it's tied to a date, not a weekday, some years it lands on a weekend and turns into an all-day event, with bars opening early, parades, and pub crawls.

**The specific risk:** starting early. Day drinking that begins at breakfast or a morning parade means many more hours of drinking than a typical night out, often with green beer, Irish car bombs (a shot dropped into a pint), and other fast drinks.

**One tip:** if you start early, pace for a marathon, not a sprint. Eat a full breakfast, keep to one drink an hour or less, and take a break in the middle of the afternoon with food and water. Our [St. Patrick's Day hangover guide](/never-hungover/st-patricks-day-hangover) covers the full day.

### Cinco de Mayo (May 5)

In the US, Cinco de Mayo has become a big margarita-and-beer day for bars and restaurants. (It commemorates the Mexican army's victory at the Battle of Puebla in 1862. It's not Mexican Independence Day, which is in September.)

**The specific risk:** strong mixed drinks. Restaurant margaritas, especially large or "top-shelf" ones, can contain two or more standard drinks each, and sweet drinks go down easily. Tequila shots on top add up fast.

**One tip:** treat each big margarita as two drinks when you're counting, and order food with your first one. If you're not sure how much alcohol is in a drink, our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) breaks down common beers, wines, and cocktails.

### Kentucky Derby Day (first Saturday in May)

Derby Day is a smaller national event but a big drinking day for many people, centered on mint juleps and all-afternoon parties. A traditional julep is mostly bourbon, so it's a strong drink that doesn't taste like one once it's sweetened and iced.

**The specific risk:** afternoon drinking in the sun with strong bourbon cocktails, then an evening of more.

**One tip:** ask for juleps light on the bourbon, alternate with water, and stay in the shade.

### Memorial Day Weekend (last weekend of May)

Memorial Day weekend is the unofficial start of summer in the US: barbecues, lakes, beaches, and three days off. That makes it less of a single "day" and more of a long weekend of repeated drinking.

**The specific risk:** heat and water. Drinking in the sun dehydrates you faster, and alcohol is a major factor in boating accidents and drownings. Alcohol affects balance, judgment, and reaction time just as much on a boat as in a car.

**One tip:** if you're operating a boat or swimming, don't drink. If you're just at the barbecue, wear sunscreen, keep a water bottle next to your drink, and plan rest days between the big ones.

### Fourth of July (July 4)

The Fourth of July is often listed as one of the top beer-sales holidays of the year, and it's a classic all-day outdoor drinking occasion: barbecues, boats, beaches, and fireworks after dark. US traffic safety officials consistently identify the July 4 holiday period as one of the deadliest times on the road because of drunk driving.

**The specific risk:** a long day in the heat, drinking from early afternoon to late night, then fireworks (handling explosives after drinking is a bad idea) and a crowded drive home.

**One tip:** pick a designated driver who is actually not drinking, not just "drinking less." Keep alcohol away from anyone handling fireworks, and eat real food early in the day, not only late at night. For hot-weather drinking, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

### Labor Day Weekend (first weekend of September)

Labor Day weekend closes out the summer the same way Memorial Day opens it: three days of cookouts, travel, and parties. It's also a major US enforcement period, with national "Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over" campaigns running around it.

**The specific risk:** the same as Memorial Day, plus end-of-summer travel back home on Monday, sometimes while still tired or hungover.

**One tip:** if you're driving home on Monday, keep Sunday night light. Alcohol can still affect you the next morning after a heavy night.

### Halloween (October 31, plus the weekend nearest it)

Halloween has grown into a major adult party night, and when it falls midweek, the parties often happen the weekend before or after, which can stretch it into multiple nights.

**The specific risk:** costumes and crowds. Masks and costumes can make it harder to spot a friend who's in trouble, and Halloween is also a night with lots of pedestrians, including children, on the streets after dark. That makes driving after drinking especially dangerous.

**One tip:** keep your group together and agree on a plan for getting home. Never drive on Halloween night if you've been drinking.

### Thanksgiving Eve, or "Blackout Wednesday" (the night before Thanksgiving)

The Wednesday before Thanksgiving is widely described by bar owners as one of the busiest bar nights of the year. People are home for the holiday, run into old friends at hometown bars, and have the next day off. The nickname "Blackout Wednesday" says a lot about how it often goes.

**The specific risk:** fast, heavy drinking with friends you haven't seen in a while, rounds of shots, and then driving on unfamiliar or icy roads during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year.

**One tip:** we have a whole [Blackout Wednesday plan](/never-hungover/blackout-wednesday), and the short version is: decide your ride home first, eat dinner before you go, and skip the shots.

### The December Holiday Season (office parties through Christmas Eve)

December isn't one day but a month of drinking occasions: office parties, friend gatherings, family dinners, and Christmas Eve celebrations, building up to New Year's Eve. US traffic safety agencies run major drunk-driving enforcement campaigns from mid-December through New Year's because this stretch is consistently a high-risk period.

**The specific risk:** stacking. A party on Thursday, another on Saturday, and a family dinner on Sunday means many heavy nights close together with little recovery, plus rich food, late nights, and travel.

**One tip:** pick which events you actually want to drink at, and have a "light night" or a sober night in between. Our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach) goes deeper on getting through the season.

## The Big Drinking Days at a Glance

## Biggest Bar Night vs. Biggest Drinking Day: What's the Difference?

People often use these phrases interchangeably, but they point to different days.

**The biggest bar nights** are the ones where people go out: New Year's Eve, Thanksgiving Eve, and St. Patrick's Day are the ones bar owners mention most. These nights bring crowds, long waits, expensive rides, and lots of strangers, and the main risks are getting home safely and losing count of rounds.

**The biggest at-home drinking days** are the ones built around a party or an event on TV: Super Bowl Sunday, the Fourth of July, and family holidays. The main risks here are different. Drinks are poured more generously at home than in a bar (home pours are often much bigger than a standard drink), nobody is cutting you off, and the drive home from a friend's place is where trouble often starts.

Knowing which kind of day you're heading into helps you pick the right part of the plan below to focus on.

## Why These Days Leave Worse Hangovers

Most people notice they feel worse after a holiday than after a normal night out with a similar number of drinks. Usually it isn't really "a similar number." But even when it is, these days stack up several things that make hangovers worse:

- **Longer sessions.** Day drinking that starts at noon or a morning parade can mean ten or more hours of drinking. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults, and it can't speed up just because the party did.
- **Drinking on an empty stomach.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. On busy days people often skip meals or rely on snacks. See [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).
- **Mixing drinks.** Champagne, then beer, then shots usually means more total alcohol, and sweet mixed drinks can hide how strong a drink is.
- **Heat and sun.** Summer holidays add sweating on top of alcohol's effect of making you pee more, which worsens dehydration.
- **Lost sleep.** Late nights and alcohol both cut into good-quality sleep, and poor sleep is a big part of why the next day feels so bad.
- **Darker drinks.** Bourbon, brandy, and red wine contain more congeners (by-products of fermentation and aging) than clear spirits, and some research links them to worse hangovers at the same alcohol dose.

None of these is a mystery, which is good news: most of them are within your control with a little planning.

## A Plan That Works for Any Big Drinking Day

You don't need a different strategy for every holiday. The same plan covers all of them.

### Before you go

1. **Decide how you're getting home.** A sober driver who has agreed to not drink, a rideshare app with your payment set up, a taxi number, public transit, or a place to stay. Make this decision while you're sober, because your judgment about whether you're "fine to drive" gets worse with every drink.
2. **Eat a real meal.** Something with protein, fat, and fiber, an hour or two before you start. A meal slows alcohol absorption and makes the early drinks hit less hard.
3. **Set a rough limit.** Pick a number of drinks and a time you'll switch to water. It doesn't have to be strict, but a number you chose while sober is much easier to stick to than one you make up as you go.
4. **Charge your phone and set a meeting point.** Especially for crowds, parades, and festivals.

### While you're drinking

1. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between each alcoholic drink slows your pace and helps with fluids.
2. **Pace yourself.** Aim for about one standard drink an hour or less. In the US, one standard drink is about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits, each containing roughly 14 grams of pure alcohol.
3. **Count honestly.** Large cocktails, strong craft beers, and generous home pours can each be two drinks.
4. **Skip the shots, or limit them.** Shots raise your blood alcohol quickly, and rounds of them are a common route to blacking out. Our guide to [blacking out](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains why fast drinking is the main trigger.
5. **Keep eating.** Snacks help, a second meal helps more.
6. **Watch your friends.** If someone is getting very drunk, get them water and food and slow them down early, before it becomes an emergency.

### Before bed and the morning after

1. **Drink water before bed,** and keep a glass by the bed.
2. **Don't take acetaminophen (Tylenol) while drinking or right before bed** to "prevent" a headache. It doesn't prevent a hangover and adds work for your liver.
3. **In the morning,** have fluids with some salt and sugar, eat something easy, and rest. Time is the only real cure. Our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what helps and what doesn't.
4. **Don't drive the next morning if you drank heavily and late.** Alcohol may still be in your system. See [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system).

## Driving: The Part That Matters Most

On every one of these days, the single most important decision is how you get home. Holiday periods are when US traffic safety agencies run their biggest drunk-driving enforcement campaigns, because these are the times when alcohol-impaired crashes are most common.

A few things worth knowing:

- **You can't feel your blood alcohol level.** People routinely underestimate how impaired they are. "I feel fine" is not a reliable test. Our explainer on [BAC](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) covers why.
- **Coffee, cold showers, and food don't sober you up.** They might make you feel more alert, but only time lowers your blood alcohol.
- **The legal limit isn't a safe limit.** In most of the US it's 0.08% for adult drivers, but driving skills are affected well below that.
- **Rides are expensive and scarce at peak times.** On New Year's Eve especially, plan around surge pricing: leave earlier, leave later, or stay put.

If you're hosting, you can help: have non-alcoholic options that feel like a real drink, stop serving alcohol well before the party ends, and offer a couch to anyone who shouldn't drive.

## When It's an Emergency: Signs of Alcohol Poisoning

Big drinking days are also when emergency rooms see more alcohol-related visits. Alcohol poisoning happens when someone drinks so much, usually quickly, that the parts of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate, and temperature start to shut down. It can be fatal, and it can happen to healthy young people on a single night.

Call 911 if someone shows **any** of these signs (the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism lists them as critical signs of alcohol overdose):

- Confusion or stupor, or they can't be woken up
- Vomiting, especially while passed out or barely conscious
- Seizures
- Slow breathing (fewer than eight breaths a minute) or irregular breathing, with long gaps between breaths
- Pale or bluish skin, or a low body temperature (cold, clammy skin)

**What to do while you wait:** keep them on their side so they can't choke on vomit, stay with them, keep them warm, and don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more alcohol. Never leave someone to "sleep it off." Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone stops drinking because alcohol is still being absorbed from the stomach. Our full guide on [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) goes into more detail.

Many people hesitate to call because they worry about getting a friend in trouble. Many US states have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan laws meant to protect people who call for help in an alcohol emergency, though the details vary by state. Either way, calling is the right thing to do.

## A Note for People Who Find These Days Hard

Not everyone enjoys the big drinking days. If you're cutting back, taking medication that doesn't mix with alcohol, pregnant, driving, or just don't feel like drinking, you don't owe anyone an explanation. Holding a non-alcoholic drink, like a soda with lime or a non-alcoholic beer, tends to stop most people from offering you one.

And if you notice that holidays are becoming the main reason you drink heavily, or that you often drink more than you meant to, that's worth a private conversation with your doctor. It's a normal health question, not a confession.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take around drinking. Early research, mostly in animals plus a small amount of human data, suggests it may support how the body processes alcohol, and many people take it before or during a big night. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers outright, it does not lower your blood alcohol, and it does nothing to make driving safer. Think of it as an optional extra on top of the basics in this guide (food, water, pacing, and a ride home), not a replacement for them.

If you want to try it on your next big day, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [best DHM supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-dhm-supplements) compares them. If you take prescription medication, check with a pharmacist or doctor before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

There's no official biggest drinking day of the year, but New Year's Eve, Blackout Wednesday, St. Patrick's Day, Super Bowl Sunday, and the Fourth of July are the days most often named, with Mardi Gras, Cinco de Mayo, the summer holiday weekends, Halloween, and the December party season close behind. What they share is long sessions, lots of people drinking at once, and busy, risky roads. The plan is the same for all of them: settle your ride home first, eat before you drink, alternate with water, set a limit while you're sober, and know when a friend needs a 911 call rather than a couch.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the biggest drinking day of the year?**

There's no official measurement, so it depends on how you count. New Year's Eve is the day most often named as the biggest drinking night, especially in bars. The night before Thanksgiving (Blackout Wednesday) and St. Patrick's Day are often called the busiest bar nights, while Super Bowl Sunday and the Fourth of July are frequently cited as the biggest beer days because of at-home parties.

**What is the biggest bar night of the year?**

Bar owners most often point to New Year's Eve, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and St. Patrick's Day. Thanksgiving Eve stands out because so many people are home for the holiday, meeting old friends at hometown bars, with the next day off.

**What holiday do Americans drink the most on?**

Surveys and sales reports usually put New Year's Eve, the Fourth of July, St. Patrick's Day, Thanksgiving Eve, and Super Bowl Sunday near the top. The order changes depending on whether the source measures retail sales, bar sales, or what people say in surveys.

**Why is the night before Thanksgiving such a big drinking night?**

It's one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, so many people are back in their hometowns with old friends, most have Thursday off, and there's no family obligation until the next afternoon. That combination leads to crowded bars and fast, heavy drinking, which is how it earned the nickname Blackout Wednesday.

**Are holidays more dangerous for drunk driving?**

Yes. US traffic safety officials consistently flag holiday periods, especially the Fourth of July and the stretch from mid-December through New Year's, as high-risk times for alcohol-impaired crashes, and they run special enforcement campaigns around Labor Day and the December holidays. The safest plan is to decide how you're getting home before you start drinking.

**How do I avoid a hangover on a big drinking day?**

The only sure way is not to drink, or to drink less. Beyond that, the habits that help most are eating a real meal before you start, pacing yourself to about one drink an hour or less, alternating each drink with water, avoiding rounds of shots, and getting as much sleep as you can. There is no good evidence that any pill or supplement reliably prevents a hangover.

**Why do I feel worse after holiday drinking than a normal night out?**

Holiday drinking usually means longer sessions, earlier starts, mixed drinks, bigger home pours, less food, more heat or travel, and less sleep. Each of these makes a hangover worse, and together they add up. Often people also drink more than they realize because they lose count over a long day.

**When should I call 911 for a friend who has been drinking?**

Call if they can't be woken up, are breathing slowly or irregularly, are vomiting while passed out, have a seizure, have pale or bluish skin, or are severely confused. Turn them on their side, stay with them, and don't let them sleep it off alone. It's always better to call and not need it than the other way around.
